claim: Lipid droplets (LD) are present in early-stage somatic and germline cells within the Drosophila testis.
source: Here, we show LD are present in early-stage somatic and germline cells within the Drosophila testis.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data showing LD distribution in testis using BODIPY and LipidTox staining, and lineage-specific GFP-LD expression.

claim: Triglyceride lipase brummer (bmm) regulates testis LD.
source: We identified a role for triglyceride lipase brummer (bmm) in regulating testis LD, and found that whole-body loss of bmm leads to defects in sperm development.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing bmm1 mutants have significantly more LD and expanded LD distribution compared to controls.

claim: Whole-body loss of bmm leads to defects in sperm development.
source: We identified a role for triglyceride lipase brummer (bmm) in regulating testis LD, and found that whole-body loss of bmm leads to defects in sperm development.
evidence: Supported by data showing bmm1 males have smaller testis size, fewer spermatid bundles, and other spermatogenic defects.

claim: bmm plays a cell-autonomous role in regulating testis LD and spermatogenesis.
source: Importantly, these represent cell-autonomous roles for bmm in regulating testis LD and spermatogenesis.
evidence: Supported by FLP-FRT clone experiments showing bmm1 spermatocyte clones have significantly more LD than control clones.

claim: bmm mutants show excess triglyceride accumulation.
source: Because lipidomic analysis of bmm mutants revealed excess triglyceride accumulation, and spermatogenic defects in bmm mutants were rescued by genetically blocking triglyceride synthesis, our data suggest that bmm-mediated regulation of triglyceride influences sperm development.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry-based lipidomic profiling showing 55/97 triglyceride species were significantly higher in bmm1 males.

claim: Spermatogenic defects in bmm mutants are rescued by genetically blocking triglyceride synthesis.
source: Because lipidomic analysis of bmm mutants revealed excess triglyceride accumulation, and spermatogenic defects in bmm mutants were rescued by genetically blocking triglyceride synthesis, our data suggest that bmm-mediated regulation of triglyceride influences sperm development.
evidence: Supported by data showing mdyQX25/k03902;bmm1 males have larger testes, more spermatid bundles, and rescued GSC numbers compared to bmm1 males.

claim: bmm-mediated regulation of triglyceride influences sperm development.
source: Because lipidomic analysis of bmm mutants revealed excess triglyceride accumulation, and spermatogenic defects in bmm mutants were rescued by genetically blocking triglyceride synthesis, our data suggest that bmm-mediated regulation of triglyceride influences sperm development.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of lipidomic data showing triglyceride accumulation and genetic rescue experiments blocking triglyceride synthesis.

claim: Triglyceride is an important neutral lipid that contributes to Drosophila sperm development.
source: This identifies triglyceride as an important neutral lipid that contributes to Drosophila sperm development, and reveals a key role for bmm in regulating testis triglyceride levels during spermatogenesis.
evidence: Supported by data showing triglyceride accumulation in bmm mutants and rescue of spermatogenic defects by blocking triglyceride synthesis.

claim: bmm plays a key role in regulating testis triglyceride levels during spermatogenesis.
source: This identifies triglyceride as an important neutral lipid that contributes to Drosophila sperm development, and reveals a key role for bmm in regulating testis triglyceride levels during spermatogenesis.
evidence: Supported by lipidomic data showing triglyceride accumulation in bmm mutants and LD phenotypes in bmm mutants.

claim: Small LD (<1 μm) are present at the apical tip of the testis in w1118 males.
source: We previously reported the presence of small LD (<1 μm) at the apical tip of the testis (Wat et al., 2020), a finding we reproduced in w1118 males using neutral lipid stain BODIPY (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data using BODIPY staining and reference to previous publication.

claim: LD are present in the region that contains stem cells, early-stage somatic cells, and germline cells.
source: These LD were present in the region that contains stem cells, early-stage somatic cells, and germline cells (Figure 1A, A', arrows).
evidence: Supported by microscopy images showing LD distribution in the apical region of the testis.

claim: LD are present in the hub, an organizing center and stem cell niche in the Drosophila testis.
source: LD were also present in the hub, an organizing center and stem cell niche in the Drosophila testis (Figure 1A'', A''', arrows) (de Cuevas and Matunis, 2011), but largely absent within the area occupied by spermatocytes (Figure 1A, A', arrowheads).
evidence: Supported by microscopy images and citation to literature defining the hub.

claim: LD are largely absent within the area occupied by spermatocytes.
source: LD were also present in the hub, an organizing center and stem cell niche in the Drosophila testis (Figure 1A'', A''', arrows) (de Cuevas and Matunis, 2011), but largely absent within the area occupied by spermatocytes (Figure 1A, A', arrowheads).
evidence: Supported by microscopy images showing LD distribution.

claim: The LD distribution pattern was reproduced in two independent genetic backgrounds and at two additional ages.
source: This LD distribution was reproduced in two independent genetic backgrounds and at two additional ages (Figure 1B, C).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data from Canton S and Oregon R backgrounds at different ages.

claim: Cholesterol-binding fluorescent polyene antibiotic filipin III did not detect cholesterol within testis LD.
source: While LD may contain multiple neutral lipid species (Walther et al., 2017), cholesterol-binding fluorescent polyene antibiotic filipin III did not detect cholesterol within testis LD (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), suggesting triglyceride is the main neutral lipid in Drosophila testis LD.
evidence: Supported by filipin III staining data showing no cholesterol signal in testis LD.

claim: Triglyceride is the main neutral lipid in Drosophila testis LD.
source: While LD may contain multiple neutral lipid species (Walther et al., 2017), cholesterol-binding fluorescent polyene antibiotic filipin III did not detect cholesterol within testis LD (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), suggesting triglyceride is the main neutral lipid in Drosophila testis LD.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of cholesterol in testis LD and knowledge that LD contain neutral lipids.

claim: The majority of somatic LD in 0-day-old males are located <30 μm from the hub.
source: Somatic overexpression of UAS-GFP-LD using Traffic jam (Tj)-GAL4 revealed that the majority of somatic LD in 0-day-old males were located <30 μm from the hub (Figure 1D, E).
evidence: Supported by quantification of GFP-LD distribution in somatic cells using Tj-GAL4 driver.

claim: The somatic LD distribution coincides with a marker for somatic stem cells and their immediate daughter cells (Zfh-1).
source: Because the somatic LD distribution coincided with a marker for somatic stem cells and their immediate daughter cells (Zinc finger homeodomain 1, Zfh-1) (Figure 1F; two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test) (Leatherman and Dinardo, 2008), but not with a marker for late somatic cells (Eyes absent, Eya) (Amoyel et al., 2016; Fabrizio et al., 2003), our data suggest LD are present in early somatic cells.
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of LD distribution with Zfh-1 marker distribution and citations to literature defining these markers.

claim: The somatic LD distribution does not coincide with a marker for late somatic cells (Eya).
source: Because the somatic LD distribution coincided with a marker for somatic stem cells and their immediate daughter cells (Zinc finger homeodomain 1, Zfh-1) (Figure 1F; two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test) (Leatherman and Dinardo, 2008), but not with a marker for late somatic cells (Eyes absent, Eya) (Amoyel et al., 2016; Fabrizio et al., 2003), our data suggest LD are present in early somatic cells.
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of LD distribution with Eya marker distribution and citations to literature defining these markers.

claim: LD are present in early somatic cells.
source: Because the somatic LD distribution coincided with a marker for somatic stem cells and their immediate daughter cells (Zinc finger homeodomain 1, Zfh-1) (Figure 1F; two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test) (Leatherman and Dinardo, 2008), but not with a marker for late somatic cells (Eyes absent, Eya) (Amoyel et al., 2016; Fabrizio et al., 2003), our data suggest LD are present in early somatic cells.
evidence: Inferred from the coincidence of LD distribution with early somatic cell markers but not late somatic cell markers.

claim: Germline LD are present in cells near the apical tip of the testis in 0-day-old males.
source: Germline overexpression of UAS-GFP-LD using nanos (nos)-GAL4 demonstrated the presence of LD within germline cells near the apical tip of the testis in 0-day-old males (Figure 1G, H).
evidence: Supported by GFP-LD expression data using nos-GAL4 driver.

claim: The disappearance of germline LD coincides with peak expression of Bam-GFP.
source: Specifically, the disappearance of germline LD coincided with peak expression of a GFP reporter that reflects the expression of Bag-of-marbles (Bam) protein in the testis (Bam-GFP) (Chen and McKearin, 2003; Figure 1I, J).
evidence: Supported by spatial correlation analysis of LD distribution and Bam-GFP expression, with citation to literature on Bam-GFP reporter.

claim: Peak Bam expression signals the last round of transient amplifying mitotic cell cycle prior to the germline's transition into the meiotic cell cycle.
source: Because peak Bam expression signals the last round of transient amplifying mitotic cell cycle prior to the germline's transition into the meiotic cell cycle (Insco et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2014b; Gönczy et al., 1997), our data suggest that germline LD, like somatic LD, are present in cells at early stages of development.
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on Bam function.

claim: Germline LD, like somatic LD, are present in cells at early stages of development.
source: Because peak Bam expression signals the last round of transient amplifying mitotic cell cycle prior to the germline's transition into the meiotic cell cycle (Insco et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2014b; Gönczy et al., 1997), our data suggest that germline LD, like somatic LD, are present in cells at early stages of development.
evidence: Inferred from the coincidence of LD disappearance with peak Bam expression, which marks a specific developmental transition.

claim: Adipose triglyceride lipase (ATGL) is a critical regulator of neutral lipid metabolism and LD.
source: Adipose triglyceride lipase (ATGL) is a critical regulator of neutral lipid metabolism and LD (Athenstaedt and Daum, 2003; Chitraju et al., 2013; Grönke et al., 2005; Haemmerle et al., 2006; Haemmerle et al., 2011; Huijsman et al., 2009; Korbelius et al., 2019; Kurat et al., 2006; Zimmermann et al., 2004; Attané et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to literature on ATGL function.

claim: Loss of ATGL in many cell types triggers LD accumulation.
source: Loss of ATGL in many cell types triggers LD accumulation, and ATGL overexpression decreases LD number (Grönke et al., 2007; Grönke et al., 2005; Haemmerle et al., 2006; Korbelius et al., 2019; Zimmermann et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2014; Tuohetahuntila et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to literature on ATGL function.

claim: ATGL overexpression decreases LD number.
source: Loss of ATGL in many cell types triggers LD accumulation, and ATGL overexpression decreases LD number (Grönke et al., 2007; Grönke et al., 2005; Haemmerle et al., 2006; Korbelius et al., 2019; Zimmermann et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2014; Tuohetahuntila et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to literature on ATGL function.

claim: The Drosophila ATGL homolog brummer (bmm) regulates testis LD induced by mitochondrial stress.
source: Given that the Drosophila ATGL homolog brummer (bmm) regulates testis LD induced by mitochondrial stress (Sênos Demarco et al., 2019), we explored whether bmm regulates testis LD under normal physiological conditions.
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on bmm function under stress conditions.

claim: GFP expression from the bmm-GFP reporter is present in the germline of testes.
source: GFP expression was present in the germline of bmm-GFP testes, and we found germline GFP levels were higher in spermatocytes than at earlier stages of sperm development (Figure 2A, B; one-way analysis of variance [ANOVA] with Tukey multiple comparison test).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data and statistical analysis of GFP intensity in different cell types.

claim: Germline GFP levels from the bmm-GFP reporter are higher in spermatocytes than at earlier stages of sperm development.
source: GFP expression was present in the germline of bmm-GFP testes, and we found germline GFP levels were higher in spermatocytes than at earlier stages of sperm development (Figure 2A, B; one-way analysis of variance [ANOVA] with Tukey multiple comparison test).
evidence: Supported by quantification of GFP intensity and statistical analysis.

claim: The expression pattern of bmm in the germline from single-cell RNA sequencing data matches the observation with the bmm-GFP reporter.
source: The expression pattern of bmm in the germline matched our observation with the bmm-GFP reporter (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by analysis of publicly available single-cell RNA sequencing data.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing data identified bmm expression in the somatic lineage that was higher in cells at later stages of development.
source: While levels of the bmm-GFP reporter were lower in somatic cells, single-cell RNA sequencing data identified bmm expression in the somatic lineage that was higher in cells at later stages of development (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by analysis of publicly available single-cell RNA sequencing data.

claim: Additional neutral lipid- and lipid droplet-associated genes such as lipid storage droplet-2, Seipin, Lipin, and midway show differential regulation during differentiation in the testis.
source: Additional neutral lipid- and lipid droplet-associated genes such as lipid storage droplet-2, Seipin, Lipin, and midway also showed differential regulation during differentiation in the testis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: Supported by analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data.

claim: bmm upregulation in both somatic and germline cells during differentiation corresponds to the downregulation of testis LD.
source: Combined with our data on the location of testis LD, these gene expression data suggest that bmm upregulation in both somatic and germline cells during differentiation corresponds to the downregulation of testis LD.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between bmm expression patterns and LD distribution data.

claim: Germline GFP levels from bmm-GFP are negatively correlated with testis LD.
source: Supporting this, germline GFP levels were negatively correlated with testis LD in bmm-GFP flies (Figure 2A, C), suggesting regions with higher bmm expression had fewer LD.
evidence: Supported by spatial correlation analysis of GFP expression and LD distribution.

claim: Regions with higher bmm expression have fewer LD.
source: Supporting this, germline GFP levels were negatively correlated with testis LD in bmm-GFP flies (Figure 2A, C), suggesting regions with higher bmm expression had fewer LD.
evidence: Inferred from the negative correlation between bmm-GFP expression and LD number.

claim: bmm1 males have significantly more LD across all LD sizes compared with control males at the apical tip of the testis.
source: bmm1 males had significantly more LD across all LD sizes compared with control males at the apical tip of the testis (Figure 2D–G; Welch two-sample t-test with Bonferroni correction) and showed a significantly expanded LD distribution (Figure 2D–F, H; two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test).
evidence: Supported by quantification of LD number and size distribution with statistical analysis.

claim: bmm1 males show a significantly expanded LD distribution.
source: bmm1 males had significantly more LD across all LD sizes compared with control males at the apical tip of the testis (Figure 2D–G; Welch two-sample t-test with Bonferroni correction) and showed a significantly expanded LD distribution (Figure 2D–F, H; two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test).
evidence: Supported by spatial distribution analysis with statistical testing.

claim: bmm normally restricts LD to the apical tip of the testis.
source: This suggests bmm normally restricts LD to the apical tip of the testis, an observation we confirmed in both somatic and germline lineages using lineage-specific expression of GFP-LD (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: Inferred from the expanded LD distribution in bmm mutants and confirmed by lineage-specific LD visualization.

claim: bmm1 spermatocyte clones have significantly more LD at 3 days post-clone induction compared to bmmrev clones.
source: Importantly, after inducing homozygous bmmrev or bmm1 clones in the testes using the FLP-FRT system (Figure 3A, B; Xu and Rubin, 1993), we found bmm1 spermatocyte clones had significantly more LD at 3 days post-clone induction (Figure 3C; Welch two-sample t-test), a stage at which LD were absent from bmmrev clones.
evidence: Supported by quantification of LD in clonal analysis with statistical testing.

claim: Cell-autonomous bmm loss has no significant effect on LD at any other stage of germline development besides spermatocytes.
source: Because we observed no significant effect of cell-autonomous bmm loss on LD at any other stage of germline development (Figure 3C), this suggests bmm function is not required to regulate LD at early stages of germ cell development.
evidence: Supported by quantification of LD in clones at different developmental stages.

claim: bmm function is not required to regulate LD at early stages of germ cell development.
source: Because we observed no significant effect of cell-autonomous bmm loss on LD at any other stage of germline development (Figure 3C), this suggests bmm function is not required to regulate LD at early stages of germ cell development.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of LD phenotype in bmm1 clones at early developmental stages.

claim: bmm plays a role in regulating LD at the spermatogonia–spermatocyte transition.
source: Instead, our data suggest bmm plays a role in regulating LD at the spermatogonia–spermatocyte transition.
evidence: Inferred from the specific effect of bmm loss on LD in spermatocytes but not earlier stages.

claim: bmm plays a cell-autonomous role as a regulator of LD in germline cells.
source: While we were unable to assess LD in bmm1 somatic clones, our data reveal a previously unrecognized cell-autonomous role for bmm as a regulator of LD in germline cells.
evidence: Supported by clonal analysis showing LD phenotypes in bmm1 germline clones.

claim: Testis size in 0-day-old bmm1 males is significantly smaller than in age-matched bmmrev controls.
source: In 0-day-old bmm1 males reared at 25°C, testis size was significantly smaller than in age-matched bmmrev controls (Figure 4A, B; Welch two-sample t-test), and the number of spermatid bundles was significantly lower (Figure 4C; Kruskal–Wallis rank sum test).
evidence: Supported by quantification of testis size with statistical analysis.

claim: The number of spermatid bundles in 0-day-old bmm1 males is significantly lower than in bmmrev controls.
source: In 0-day-old bmm1 males reared at 25°C, testis size was significantly smaller than in age-matched bmmrev controls (Figure 4A, B; Welch two-sample t-test), and the number of spermatid bundles was significantly lower (Figure 4C; Kruskal–Wallis rank sum test).
evidence: Supported by quantification of spermatid bundles with statistical analysis.

claim: bmm1 phenotypes are more pronounced when animals are reared at 29°C.
source: When the animals were reared at 29°C, a temperature that exacerbates spermatogenesis defects associated with changes in lipid metabolism (Ben-David et al., 2015), bmm1 phenotypes were more pronounced (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B; Welch two-sample t-test, Kruskal–Wallis rank sum test).
evidence: Supported by quantification of testis size and spermatid bundles at 29°C with citation to literature on temperature effects.

claim: Defects in testis size persist at 14 days post-eclosion in bmm1 males.
source: Defects in testis size were also observed at 14 days post-eclosion; suggesting testis size defects persist later into the life course (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C; Welch two-sample t-test).
evidence: Supported by quantification of testis size at 14 days with statistical analysis.

claim: The number of spermatid bundles is not significantly different between bmm1 and bmmrev males at 14 days post-eclosion.
source: In contrast, the number of spermatid bundles per testis was not significantly different between bmm1 and bmmrev males at this age (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D; Welch two-sample t-test), potentially due to a large decrease in the number of spermatid bundles in 14-day-old bmmrev males (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by quantification of spermatid bundles at 14 days with statistical analysis.

claim: Loss of bmm affects testis development and spermatogenesis.
source: Together, these data suggest loss of bmm affects testis development and spermatogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from the multiple phenotypes observed in bmm1 males including testis size and spermatid bundle defects.

claim: Similar phenotypes to those in bmm1 flies are observed in male mice without ATGL.
source: Similar phenotypes are observed in male mice without ATGL (Masaki et al., 2017), and supplementing the diet of bmm1 males with medium-chain triglycerides partially rescued the testis and spermatogenic defects we observed in flies (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, F; one-way ANOVA with Tukey multiple comparison test), as it does in mice (Masaki et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on ATGL-deficient mice and dietary rescue experiments in flies.

claim: Supplementing the diet of bmm1 males with medium-chain triglycerides partially rescues testis and spermatogenic defects.
source: Similar phenotypes are observed in male mice without ATGL (Masaki et al., 2017), and supplementing the diet of bmm1 males with medium-chain triglycerides partially rescued the testis and spermatogenic defects we observed in flies (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, F; one-way ANOVA with Tukey multiple comparison test), as it does in mice (Masaki et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by quantification of testis size and spermatid bundles in bmm1 males fed medium-chain triglycerides.

claim: There are similarities between flies and mice in fertility-related phenotypes associated with whole-body loss of bmm/ATGL.
source: This identifies similarities between flies and mice in fertility-related phenotypes associated with whole-body loss of bmm/ATGL.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of phenotypes in bmm1 flies and ATGL-deficient mice, and similar rescue by medium-chain triglycerides.

claim: bmm1 males have a significant increase in the number of GSCs compared to bmmrev males.
source: We observed a significant increase in the number of GSCs (Figure 4F; Kruskal–Wallis rank sum test) and higher variability in GSC number in bmm1 males (p = 5.7 × 10−12 by F-test).
evidence: Supported by quantification of GSC number with statistical analysis.

claim: bmm1 males show higher variability in GSC number compared to bmmrev males.
source: We observed a significant increase in the number of GSCs (Figure 4F; Kruskal–Wallis rank sum test) and higher variability in GSC number in bmm1 males (p = 5.7 × 10−12 by F-test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of GSC number variance.

claim: Hub size in bmm1 testes is significantly larger than in testes from bmmrev controls.
source: While hub size in bmm1 testes was significantly larger than in testes from bmmrev controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G, H; Welch two-sample t-test), the number of phosphohistone H3-positive GSCs, which indicates proliferating GSCs, was unchanged in bmm1 animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I; Kruskal–Wallis rank sum test).
evidence: Supported by quantification of hub area with statistical analysis.

claim: The number of phosphohistone H3-positive GSCs is unchanged in bmm1 animals.
source: While hub size in bmm1 testes was significantly larger than in testes from bmmrev controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G, H; Welch two-sample t-test), the number of phosphohistone H3-positive GSCs, which indicates proliferating GSCs, was unchanged in bmm1 animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I; Kruskal–Wallis rank sum test).
evidence: Supported by quantification of phospho-H3 positive GSCs with statistical analysis.

claim: A larger hub may partly explain bmm's effect on GSC number.
source: While this indicates a larger hub may partly explain bmm's effect on GSC number, bmm also plays a cell-autonomous role in regulating GSCs, as we recovered a higher proportion of bmm1 clones in the GSC pool compared with bmmrev clones at 14 days after clone induction (Figure 4G; Welch two-sample t-test).
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between hub size and GSC number.

claim: bmm plays a cell-autonomous role in regulating GSCs.
source: While this indicates a larger hub may partly explain bmm's effect on GSC number, bmm also plays a cell-autonomous role in regulating GSCs, as we recovered a higher proportion of bmm1 clones in the GSC pool compared with bmmrev clones at 14 days after clone induction (Figure 4G; Welch two-sample t-test).
evidence: Supported by clonal analysis showing higher proportion of bmm1 clones in GSC pool.

claim: A higher proportion of bmm1 clones are recovered in the GSC pool compared with bmmrev clones at 14 days after clone induction.
source: While this indicates a larger hub may partly explain bmm's effect on GSC number, bmm also plays a cell-autonomous role in regulating GSCs, as we recovered a higher proportion of bmm1 clones in the GSC pool compared with bmmrev clones at 14 days after clone induction (Figure 4G; Welch two-sample t-test).
evidence: Supported by quantification of clone proportion in GSC pool with statistical analysis.

claim: Peak Bam-GFP expression in germline cells is significantly further away from the hub in bmm1 testes compared to bmmrev testes.
source: Peak Bam-GFP expression in germline cells of the testes from 0-day-old bmm1 and bmmrev males showed GFP-positive cysts were significantly further away from the hub in bmm1 testes (Figure 4H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1J; Welch two-sample t-test).
evidence: Supported by quantification of distance from hub to peak Bam-GFP expression with statistical analysis.

claim: 15/18 bmm1 testes contain Vasa-positive cysts with large nuclei in the distal half of the testis, a phenotype not present in bmmrev testes (0/8).
source: Indeed, 15/18 bmm1 testes contained Vasa-positive cysts with large nuclei in the distal half of the testis (Figure 4I, arrows), a phenotype not present in bmmrev testes (0/8) (p = 0.0005 by Pearson's Chi-square test).
evidence: Supported by microscopy observations and statistical analysis.

claim: Most bmm1 testes contain post-meiotic cells in males raised at 25°C.
source: Most bmm1 testes contained post-meiotic cells in males raised at 25°C (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K); however, germline development did not progress past the spermatocyte stage in most bmm1 testes from animals raised at 29°C (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: Supported by assessment of developmental stages reached in bmm1 testes at different temperatures.

claim: Germline development does not progress past the spermatocyte stage in most bmm1 testes from animals raised at 29°C.
source: Most bmm1 testes contained post-meiotic cells in males raised at 25°C (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K); however, germline development did not progress past the spermatocyte stage in most bmm1 testes from animals raised at 29°C (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: Supported by assessment of developmental stages reached in bmm1 testes at 29°C.

claim: Testes from bmm1 males reared at 25°C have a smaller Boule-positive area compared to bmmrev males.
source: Testes from bmm1 males reared at 25°C also had a smaller Boule-positive area (Figure 4J, Figure 4—figure supplement 1L; Welch two-sample t-test) and fewer individualization complexes and waste bags (Figure 4—figure supplement 1M, N; Kruskal–Wallis rank sum test).
evidence: Supported by quantification of Boule-positive area with statistical analysis.

claim: Testes from bmm1 males have fewer individualization complexes and waste bags compared to bmmrev males.
source: Testes from bmm1 males reared at 25°C also had a smaller Boule-positive area (Figure 4J, Figure 4—figure supplement 1L; Welch two-sample t-test) and fewer individualization complexes and waste bags (Figure 4—figure supplement 1M, N; Kruskal–Wallis rank sum test).
evidence: Supported by quantification of individualization complexes and waste bags with statistical analysis.

claim: Loss of bmm causes a reduction in differentiated cell types.
source: Because Boule-positive area, individualization complexes, and waste bags are all markers for later stages in sperm development, these data indicate that loss of bmm caused a reduction in differentiated cell types.
evidence: Inferred from the reduction in multiple markers of late-stage sperm development in bmm1 males.

claim: There are significantly fewer bmm1 spermatocyte and spermatid clones at 14 days after clone induction compared to bmmrev clones.
source: Because we observed significantly fewer bmm1 spermatocyte and spermatid clones at 14 days after clone induction (Figure 4K, L; p = 0.0496, Kruskal–Wallis rank sum test), these effects on germline development may represent a cell-autonomous role for bmm in regulating spermatogenesis in this cell type.
evidence: Supported by quantification of clone numbers with statistical analysis.

claim: The effects of bmm loss on germline development may represent a cell-autonomous role for bmm in regulating spermatogenesis in spermatocytes and spermatids.
source: Because we observed significantly fewer bmm1 spermatocyte and spermatid clones at 14 days after clone induction (Figure 4K, L; p = 0.0496, Kruskal–Wallis rank sum test), these effects on germline development may represent a cell-autonomous role for bmm in regulating spermatogenesis in this cell type.
evidence: Inferred from the reduction in bmm1 clones at later developmental stages.

claim: There is no difference in the ratio of Zfh-1-positive cells between homozygous clones and heterozygous clones in animals carrying the bmm1 or bmmrev alleles at 14 days post-clone induction.
source: While there was no difference in the ratio of Zfh-1-positive cells between homozygous clones and heterozygous clones in animals carrying the bmm1 or bmmrev alleles at 14 days post-clone induction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1O; Kruskal–Wallis rank sum test), the distance from the hub to the Zfh-1-positive clones was significantly decreased in bmm1 homozygous clones (Figure 4—figure supplement 1P; Kruskal–Wallis rank sum test).
evidence: Supported by quantification of Zfh-1-positive clone proportions with statistical analysis.

claim: The distance from the hub to Zfh-1-positive clones is significantly decreased in bmm1 homozygous clones.
source: While there was no difference in the ratio of Zfh-1-positive cells between homozygous clones and heterozygous clones in animals carrying the bmm1 or bmmrev alleles at 14 days post-clone induction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1O; Kruskal–Wallis rank sum test), the distance from the hub to the Zfh-1-positive clones was significantly decreased in bmm1 homozygous clones (Figure 4—figure supplement 1P; Kruskal–Wallis rank sum test).
evidence: Supported by quantification of clone location with statistical analysis.

claim: bmm may play a cell-autonomous role in germline cells to regulate spermatogenesis.
source: Together, these data indicate bmm may play a cell-autonomous role in germline cells, and potentially a non-cell-autonomous role in somatic cells, to regulate spermatogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from the clonal analysis data showing effects in germline clones.

claim: bmm may play a non-cell-autonomous role in somatic cells to regulate spermatogenesis.
source: Together, these data indicate bmm may play a cell-autonomous role in germline cells, and potentially a non-cell-autonomous role in somatic cells, to regulate spermatogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from the somatic clone data showing altered location of Zfh-1-positive clones.

claim: ATGL catalyzes the first and rate-limiting step of triglyceride hydrolysis.
source: ATGL catalyzes the first and rate-limiting step of triglyceride hydrolysis (Zimmermann et al., 2004; Eichmann et al., 2012; Schweiger et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on ATGL enzymatic function.

claim: Loss of ATGL or its homologs leads to excess triglyceride accumulation.
source: Loss of this enzyme or its homologs leads to excess triglyceride accumulation (Wat et al., 2020; Grönke et al., 2007; Grönke et al., 2005; Zimmermann et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2014) and shifts in multiple lipid classes (Chitraju et al., 2013; Missaglia et al., 2017; Williams et al., 1991; Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to literature on ATGL loss-of-function phenotypes.

claim: Loss of ATGL or its homologs causes shifts in multiple lipid classes.
source: Loss of this enzyme or its homologs leads to excess triglyceride accumulation (Wat et al., 2020; Grönke et al., 2007; Grönke et al., 2005; Zimmermann et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2014) and shifts in multiple lipid classes (Chitraju et al., 2013; Missaglia et al., 2017; Williams et al., 1991; Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to literature on ATGL loss-of-function phenotypes.

claim: bmm1 and bmmrev males show distinct lipidomic profiles based on hierarchical clustering.
source: Hierarchical clustering of lipid species suggests that bmm1 and bmmrev males show distinct lipidomic profiles (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by hierarchical clustering analysis of lipidomic data.

claim: 2464 and 1144 lipid features were detected with high quantitative confidence in positive and negative ion modes, respectively.
source: Overall, we detected 2464 and 1144 lipid features with high quantitative confidence in positive and negative ion modes, respectively.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: 293 unique lipid species were confirmed by matching experimental m/z, isotopic ratio, and tandem MS spectra to lipid libraries.
source: By matching experimental m/z, isotopic ratio, and tandem MS spectra to lipid libraries, we confirmed 293 unique lipid species (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry analysis and lipid identification methods.

claim: 107 lipids have a significant change in abundance between bmm1 and bmmrev males (padj < 0.05).
source: We found 107 lipids had a significant change in abundance between bmm1 and bmmrev males (padj < 0.05): 85 species were upregulated in bmm1 males and 22 lipid species were downregulated.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of lipidomic data.

claim: 85 lipid species are upregulated in bmm1 males compared to bmmrev males.
source: We found 107 lipids had a significant change in abundance between bmm1 and bmmrev males (padj < 0.05): 85 species were upregulated in bmm1 males and 22 lipid species were downregulated.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of lipidomic data.

claim: 22 lipid species are downregulated in bmm1 males compared to bmmrev males.
source: We found 107 lipids had a significant change in abundance between bmm1 and bmmrev males (padj < 0.05): 85 species were upregulated in bmm1 males and 22 lipid species were downregulated.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of lipidomic data.

claim: Triglyceride is the lipid class most affected by loss of bmm.
source: Among differentially regulated species from different lipid classes, triglyceride had the largest residual above expected proportion (p = 5.00 × 10−4 by Pearson's Chi-squared test). This suggests triglyceride was the lipid class most affected by loss of bmm (Figure 5B, C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of lipid class representation among differentially regulated species.

claim: The majority of triglyceride species (55/97) are significantly higher in abundance in bmm1 males compared to bmmrev males.
source: In bmm1 males, the majority of triglyceride species (55/97) were significantly higher in abundance compared with bmmrev control males.
evidence: Supported by lipidomic analysis showing increased triglyceride levels.

claim: There is a positive correlation between the fold increase in triglyceride abundance and the number of double bonds in bmm1 males.
source: Because we observed a positive correlation between the fold increase in triglyceride abundance with both the number of double bonds (p = 7.52 × 10−8 by Kendall's rank correlation test; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and the number of carbons (p = 2.77 × 10−10 by Kendall's rank correlation test; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), our data align well with bmm/ATGL's known role in regulating triglyceride levels (Grönke et al., 2005; Haemmerle et al., 2006; Zimmermann et al., 2004) and its substrate preference of long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (Eichmann et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of lipidomic data.

claim: There is a positive correlation between the fold increase in triglyceride abundance and the number of carbons in bmm1 males.
source: Because we observed a positive correlation between the fold increase in triglyceride abundance with both the number of double bonds (p = 7.52 × 10−8 by Kendall's rank correlation test; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and the number of carbons (p = 2.77 × 10−10 by Kendall's rank correlation test; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), our data align well with bmm/ATGL's known role in regulating triglyceride levels (Grönke et al., 2005; Haemmerle et al., 2006; Zimmermann et al., 2004) and its substrate preference of long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (Eichmann et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of lipidomic data.

claim: The lipidomic data align well with bmm/ATGL's known role in regulating triglyceride levels.
source: Because we observed a positive correlation between the fold increase in triglyceride abundance with both the number of double bonds (p = 7.52 × 10−8 by Kendall's rank correlation test; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and the number of carbons (p = 2.77 × 10−10 by Kendall's rank correlation test; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), our data align well with bmm/ATGL's known role in regulating triglyceride levels (Grönke et al., 2005; Haemmerle et al., 2006; Zimmermann et al., 2004) and its substrate preference of long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (Eichmann et al., 2012).
evidence: Inferred from the correlation patterns observed in the lipidomic data and citations to literature on ATGL function.

claim: The lipidomic data align well with bmm/ATGL's substrate preference of long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids.
source: Because we observed a positive correlation between the fold increase in triglyceride abundance with both the number of double bonds (p = 7.52 × 10−8 by Kendall's rank correlation test; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and the number of carbons (p = 2.77 × 10−10 by Kendall's rank correlation test; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), our data align well with bmm/ATGL's known role in regulating triglyceride levels (Grönke et al., 2005; Haemmerle et al., 2006; Zimmermann et al., 2004) and its substrate preference of long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (Eichmann et al., 2012).
evidence: Inferred from the correlation patterns observed in the lipidomic data and citation to literature on ATGL substrate preference.

claim: Changes in species such as fatty acids, acylcarnitine, and membrane lipids were detected in bmm1 males.
source: While we also detected changes in species such as fatty acids, acylcarnitine, and membrane lipids (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–H), in line with recent Drosophila lipidomic data (Nazario-Yepiz et al., 2021; Giedt et al., 2021), the striking accumulation of triglyceride in bmm1 males suggested that excess testis triglyceride in bmm1 males may contribute to their spermatogenic defects.
evidence: Supported by lipidomic analysis and citations to recent literature.

claim: Excess testis triglyceride in bmm1 males may contribute to their spermatogenic defects.
source: While we also detected changes in species such as fatty acids, acylcarnitine, and membrane lipids (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–H), in line with recent Drosophila lipidomic data (Nazario-Yepiz et al., 2021; Giedt et al., 2021), the striking accumulation of triglyceride in bmm1 males suggested that excess testis triglyceride in bmm1 males may contribute to their spermatogenic defects.
evidence: Inferred from the prominent triglyceride accumulation phenotype in bmm1 males.

claim: mdy is the Drosophila homolog of diacylglycerol O-acyltransferase 1 (DGAT1).
source: mdy is the Drosophila homolog of diacylglycerol O-acyltransferase 1 (DGAT1), and whole-body loss of mdy reduces whole-body triglyceride levels (Beller et al., 2010; Buszczak et al., 2002; Martínez et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on mdy/DGAT1.

claim: Whole-body loss of mdy reduces whole-body triglyceride levels.
source: mdy is the Drosophila homolog of diacylglycerol O-acyltransferase 1 (DGAT1), and whole-body loss of mdy reduces whole-body triglyceride levels (Beller et al., 2010; Buszczak et al., 2002; Martínez et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on mdy function.

claim: Testes from mdyQX25/k03902;bmm1 males have fewer LD than testes from bmm1 males.
source: Importantly, testes isolated from males with global loss of both bmm and mdy (mdyQX25/k03902;bmm1) had fewer LD than testes dissected from bmm1 males (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1I; one-way ANOVA with Tukey multiple comparison test).
evidence: Supported by quantification of LD number with statistical analysis.

claim: Testes from mdyQX25/k03902;bmm1 males are significantly larger than testes from bmm1 males.
source: We found that testes isolated from mdyQX25/k03902;bmm1 males were significantly larger and had more spermatid bundles than testes from bmm1 males (Figure 5E–G; one-way ANOVA with Tukey multiple comparison test).
evidence: Supported by quantification of testis size with statistical analysis.

claim: Testes from mdyQX25/k03902;bmm1 males have more spermatid bundles than testes from bmm1 males.
source: We found that testes isolated from mdyQX25/k03902;bmm1 males were significantly larger and had more spermatid bundles than testes from bmm1 males (Figure 5E–G; one-way ANOVA with Tukey multiple comparison test).
evidence: Supported by quantification of spermatid bundles with statistical analysis.

claim: The elevated number of GSCs in bmm1 male testes is rescued in mdyQX25/k03902;bmm1 males.
source: The elevated number of GSCs in bmm1 male testes was similarly rescued in mdyQX25/k03902;bmm1 males (Figure 5H; one-way ANOVA with Tukey multiple comparison test).
evidence: Supported by quantification of GSC number with statistical analysis.

claim: Defective spermatogenesis in bmm1 males can be partly attributed to excess triglyceride accumulation.
source: These data suggest that defective spermatogenesis in bmm1 males can be partly attributed to excess triglyceride accumulation.
evidence: Inferred from the rescue of spermatogenic defects by blocking triglyceride synthesis.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of mdy in the germline of bmm1 males partially rescues defects in testis size.
source: Notably, at least some of the effects of global mdy loss on bmm1 males can be attributed to the germline: RNAi-mediated knockdown of mdy in the germline of bmm1 males partially rescued the defects in testis size (Figure 5I; Kruskal–Wallis rank sum test with Dunn's multiple comparison test) and GSC variance (Figure 5—figure supplement 1J; p = 4.5 × 10−5 and 8.2 × 10−3 by F-test from the GAL4- and UAS-only crosses, respectively).
evidence: Supported by quantification of testis size in germline-specific mdy knockdown with statistical analysis.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of mdy in the germline of bmm1 males partially rescues GSC variance.
source: Notably, at least some of the effects of global mdy loss on bmm1 males can be attributed to the germline: RNAi-mediated knockdown of mdy in the germline of bmm1 males partially rescued the defects in testis size (Figure 5I; Kruskal–Wallis rank sum test with Dunn's multiple comparison test) and GSC variance (Figure 5—figure supplement 1J; p = 4.5 × 10−5 and 8.2 × 10−3 by F-test from the GAL4- and UAS-only crosses, respectively).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of GSC number variance.

claim: At least some of the effects of global mdy loss on bmm1 males can be attributed to the germline.
source: Notably, at least some of the effects of global mdy loss on bmm1 males can be attributed to the germline: RNAi-mediated knockdown of mdy in the germline of bmm1 males partially rescued the defects in testis size (Figure 5I; Kruskal–Wallis rank sum test with Dunn's multiple comparison test) and GSC variance (Figure 5—figure supplement 1J; p = 4.5 × 10−5 and 8.2 × 10−3 by F-test from the GAL4- and UAS-only crosses, respectively).
evidence: Inferred from the partial rescue of phenotypes by germline-specific mdy knockdown.

claim: bmm-mediated regulation of testis triglyceride plays a previously unrecognized role in regulating sperm development.
source: While future studies will need to test whether germline-specific loss of mdy also rescues spermatid number defects in bmm1 males, our data suggest bmm-mediated regulation of testis triglyceride plays a previously unrecognized role in regulating sperm development.
evidence: Inferred from the rescue experiments showing that blocking triglyceride synthesis rescues spermatogenic defects.

claim: Lipids play an essential role in regulating spermatogenesis across animals.
source: Lipids play an essential role in regulating spermatogenesis across animals (Brill et al., 2016; Keber et al., 2013; Rato et al., 2012; Wang and Huang, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on lipid roles in spermatogenesis.

claim: Studies in Drosophila have illuminated key roles for multiple lipid species in regulating sperm development.
source: Studies in Drosophila have illuminated key roles for multiple lipid species in regulating sperm development (de Cuevas and Matunis, 2011; Demarco et al., 2014; Fabian and Brill, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on lipid roles in Drosophila spermatogenesis.

claim: Phosphatidylinositol and its phosphorylated derivatives participate in diverse aspects of Drosophila spermatogenesis including meiotic cytokinesis.
source: For example, phosphatidylinositol and its phosphorylated derivatives participate in diverse aspects of Drosophila spermatogenesis including meiotic cytokinesis (Brill et al., 2016; Brill et al., 2000; Giansanti et al., 2006; Wong et al., 2005; Wong et al., 2007), somatic cell differentiation (Amoyel et al., 2016), germline and somatic cell polarity maintenance (Fairchild et al., 2017; Inaba et al., 2015; Krahn et al., 2010; Papagiannouli et al., 2019), and germline stem cell (GSC) maintenance and proliferation (Ueishi et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to literature on phosphatidylinositol function in spermatogenesis.

claim: Phosphatidylinositol and its phosphorylated derivatives participate in somatic cell differentiation during Drosophila spermatogenesis.
source: For example, phosphatidylinositol and its phosphorylated derivatives participate in diverse aspects of Drosophila spermatogenesis including meiotic cytokinesis (Brill et al., 2016; Brill et al., 2000; Giansanti et al., 2006; Wong et al., 2005; Wong et al., 2007), somatic cell differentiation (Amoyel et al., 2016), germline and somatic cell polarity maintenance (Fairchild et al., 2017; Inaba et al., 2015; Krahn et al., 2010; Papagiannouli et al., 2019), and germline stem cell (GSC) maintenance and proliferation (Ueishi et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on phosphatidylinositol function in somatic cell differentiation.

claim: Phosphatidylinositol and its phosphorylated derivatives participate in germline and somatic cell polarity maintenance during Drosophila spermatogenesis.
source: For example, phosphatidylinositol and its phosphorylated derivatives participate in diverse aspects of Drosophila spermatogenesis including meiotic cytokinesis (Brill et al., 2016; Brill et al., 2000; Giansanti et al., 2006; Wong et al., 2005; Wong et al., 2007), somatic cell differentiation (Amoyel et al., 2016), germline and somatic cell polarity maintenance (Fairchild et al., 2017; Inaba et al., 2015; Krahn et al., 2010; Papagiannouli et al., 2019), and germline stem cell (GSC) maintenance and proliferation (Ueishi et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to literature on phosphatidylinositol function in cell polarity.

claim: Phosphatidylinositol and its phosphorylated derivatives participate in GSC maintenance and proliferation during Drosophila spermatogenesis.
source: For example, phosphatidylinositol and its phosphorylated derivatives participate in diverse aspects of Drosophila spermatogenesis including meiotic cytokinesis (Brill et al., 2016; Brill et al., 2000; Giansanti et al., 2006; Wong et al., 2005; Wong et al., 2007), somatic cell differentiation (Amoyel et al., 2016), germline and somatic cell polarity maintenance (Fairchild et al., 2017; Inaba et al., 2015; Krahn et al., 2010; Papagiannouli et al., 2019), and germline stem cell (GSC) maintenance and proliferation (Ueishi et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on phosphatidylinositol function in GSC regulation.

claim: Membrane lipids influence sperm development.
source: Membrane lipids also influence sperm development (Phan et al., 2007; Steinhauer et al., 2009), whereas fatty acids play a role in processes such as meiotic cytokinesis (Szafer-Glusman et al., 2008) and sperm individualization (Ben-David et al., 2015; Jung et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on membrane lipid roles in spermatogenesis.

claim: Fatty acids play a role in meiotic cytokinesis during Drosophila spermatogenesis.
source: Membrane lipids also influence sperm development (Phan et al., 2007; Steinhauer et al., 2009), whereas fatty acids play a role in processes such as meiotic cytokinesis (Szafer-Glusman et al., 2008) and sperm individualization (Ben-David et al., 2015; Jung et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on fatty acid roles in meiotic cytokinesis.

claim: Fatty acids play a role in sperm individualization during Drosophila spermatogenesis.
source: Membrane lipids also influence sperm development (Phan et al., 2007; Steinhauer et al., 2009), whereas fatty acids play a role in processes such as meiotic cytokinesis (Szafer-Glusman et al., 2008) and sperm individualization (Ben-David et al., 2015; Jung et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on fatty acid roles in sperm individualization.

claim: Some roles for membrane lipids and fatty acids during Drosophila spermatogenesis are conserved in mammals.
source: While these studies suggest key roles for membrane lipids and fatty acids during Drosophila spermatogenesis, some of which are conserved in mammals (Rabionet et al., 2015; Santiago Valtierra et al., 2018; Zadravec et al., 2011), much less is known about how neutral lipids contribute to spermatogenesis.
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on lipid roles in mammalian spermatogenesis.

claim: Much less is known about how neutral lipids contribute to spermatogenesis compared to membrane lipids and fatty acids.
source: While these studies suggest key roles for membrane lipids and fatty acids during Drosophila spermatogenesis, some of which are conserved in mammals (Rabionet et al., 2015; Santiago Valtierra et al., 2018; Zadravec et al., 2011), much less is known about how neutral lipids contribute to spermatogenesis.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Neutral lipids are a major lipid group that includes triglyceride and cholesterol ester.
source: Neutral lipids are a major lipid group that includes triglyceride and cholesterol ester, where neutral lipids reside within specialized organelles called lipid droplets (LD) (Walther and Farese, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on neutral lipid composition and localization.

claim: Neutral lipids reside within specialized organelles called lipid droplets (LD).
source: Neutral lipids are a major lipid group that includes triglyceride and cholesterol ester, where neutral lipids reside within specialized organelles called lipid droplets (LD) (Walther and Farese, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on LD structure and function.

claim: LD are found in diverse cell types including adipocytes, muscle, liver, glia, and neurons.
source: LD are found in diverse cell types (e.g. adipocytes, muscle, liver, glia, and neurons) (Wat et al., 2020; Thiele and Spandl, 2008; Walther and Farese, 2012), and play key roles in maintaining cellular lipid homeostasis.
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on LD distribution across cell types.

claim: LD play key roles in maintaining cellular lipid homeostasis.
source: LD are found in diverse cell types (e.g. adipocytes, muscle, liver, glia, and neurons) (Wat et al., 2020; Thiele and Spandl, 2008; Walther and Farese, 2012), and play key roles in maintaining cellular lipid homeostasis.
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on LD function.

claim: In nongonadal cell types, correct regulation of LD contributes to cellular energy production.
source: In nongonadal cell types, correct regulation of LD contributes to cellular energy production (Bosma, 2016; Grönke et al., 2007; Rambold et al., 2015), sequestration and redistribution of lipid precursors (Dichlberger et al., 2014; Mitsche et al., 2018; Rajakumari et al., 2010; Schlager et al., 2015; Zanghellini et al., 2008), and regulation of lipid toxicity (Bailey et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2017; Nguyen et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on LD roles in energy metabolism.

claim: In nongonadal cell types, correct regulation of LD contributes to sequestration and redistribution of lipid precursors.
source: In nongonadal cell types, correct regulation of LD contributes to cellular energy production (Bosma, 2016; Grönke et al., 2007; Rambold et al., 2015), sequestration and redistribution of lipid precursors (Dichlberger et al., 2014; Mitsche et al., 2018; Rajakumari et al., 2010; Schlager et al., 2015; Zanghellini et al., 2008), and regulation of lipid toxicity (Bailey et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2017; Nguyen et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on LD roles in lipid precursor metabolism.

claim: In nongonadal cell types, correct regulation of LD contributes to regulation of lipid toxicity.
source: In nongonadal cell types, correct regulation of LD contributes to cellular energy production (Bosma, 2016; Grönke et al., 2007; Rambold et al., 2015), sequestration and redistribution of lipid precursors (Dichlberger et al., 2014; Mitsche et al., 2018; Rajakumari et al., 2010; Schlager et al., 2015; Zanghellini et al., 2008), and regulation of lipid toxicity (Bailey et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2017; Nguyen et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on LD roles in lipid toxicity regulation.

claim: Dysregulation of LD causes defects in cell differentiation, survival, and energy production.
source: The importance of LD to normal cellular function in nongonadal cell types is shown by the fact that dysregulation of LD causes defects in cell differentiation, survival, and energy production (Walther and Farese, 2012; Bailey et al., 2015; Henne, 2019; Welte, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on LD dysregulation phenotypes.

claim: In the testis, much less is known about the regulation and function of neutral lipids and LD, and how this regulation affects sperm development.
source: In the testis, much less is known about the regulation and function of neutral lipids and LD, and how this regulation affects sperm development.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Genes that encode proteins associated with neutral lipid metabolism and LD are expressed in the testis across multiple species.
source: First, genes that encode proteins associated with neutral lipid metabolism and LD are expressed in the testis across multiple species (Casado et al., 2013; El-Shehawi et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on gene expression in the testis.

claim: Testis LD have been identified in mammals and flies under both normal physiological conditions and after mitochondrial stress.
source: Second, testis LD have been identified in mammals and flies under both normal physiological conditions (Wat et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2015; Bajpai et al., 1998; Kerr and De Kretser, 1975; Mori and Christensen, 1980; Paniagua et al., 1987) and after mitochondrial stress (Sênos Demarco et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on testis LD identification.

claim: Loss of genes associated with neutral lipid metabolism and LD cause subfertility phenotypes in both flies and mammals.
source: Third, loss of genes associated with neutral lipid metabolism and LD cause subfertility phenotypes in both flies and mammals (Wat et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2014a; Hermo et al., 2008; Masaki et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on subfertility phenotypes.

claim: Studies suggest that mammalian testis LD contribute to steroidogenesis.
source: While studies suggest that mammalian testis LD contribute to steroidogenesis (Wang et al., 2017), the spatial, temporal, and cell-type-specific requirements for neutral lipids and LD in the testis have not been explored in detail in any animal.
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on mammalian testis LD function.

claim: The spatial, temporal, and cell-type-specific requirements for neutral lipids and LD in the testis have not been explored in detail in any animal.
source: While studies suggest that mammalian testis LD contribute to steroidogenesis (Wang et al., 2017), the spatial, temporal, and cell-type-specific requirements for neutral lipids and LD in the testis have not been explored in detail in any animal.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: It remains unclear which genes are responsible for regulating neutral lipids and LD during spermatogenesis.
source: It remains similarly unclear which genes are responsible for regulating neutral lipids and LD during spermatogenesis.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.
